# Summary: Education in Poland
Education in Poland is compulsory and typically begins with eight years of primary school, starting at age seven (or six, with pre-school attendance). Prior to the 2016 educational reform, students attended six years of primary school followed by three years of junior high (gimnazjum), but the reform abolished gimnazjum and reinstated an eight-year primary curriculum. After primary education, students move to upper secondary education, which includes several options: general secondary schools (liceum) culminating in the Matura exam for university entry; technical schools (technikum) offering five-year programs also ending in the Matura; basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa) providing three-year occupational training; and profiled vocational programs tailored to specific trades. Special schools serve students with disabilities and may also prepare them for the Matura.
Tertiary education in Poland follows the Bologna framework, with three-year bachelor’s degrees followed by two-year master's degrees, and some long-cycle master's programs for fields like medicine and pharmacy. Doctoral programs generally last about three years. Teacher training for primary schools is typically a three-year college program. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest pass), with assessments conducted each semester. Vocational education at the post-secondary level is handled by specialized schools with programs lasting about two and a half years. Reforms, notably those in 1999 and 2017, have restructured school organization, improved subject focus, and contributed to high international rankings for Polish students in reading, science, and mathematics.
